content: The National Blood Service (NBS) is the organization responsible for collecting blood and other tissues, testing, processing, and supplying them to hospitals across England and North Wales. In Scotland, these functions are carried out by a separate entity known as the Scottish National Blood Transfusion Service, which is accountable to the Scottish Executive. The NBS operates as part of a National Health Service (NHS) Special Health Authority called NHS Blood and Transplant. This authority also includes the Bio Products Laboratory, which provides blood products to hospitals, and UK Transplant, which manages the national organ donor register. The service was originally established in 1946 as the Blood Transfusion Service. In 1991, its name was changed to reflect its transition from a regionally based service to a nationally organized one. The NBS processes approximately one million blood donations annually and supplies around 8,000 units of blood daily. In 2006, service directors proposed a reorganization strategy to centralize operations by closing most local processing and testing laboratories and consolidating activities into three large supercentres to serve the same geographical area. However, this strategy faced opposition from staff and is currently under review. The future structure of NBS blood processing and testing operations remains undecided. The NBS relies entirely on voluntary blood donations from the public. Blood donation sessions are organized nationwide in various venues, including village halls, mobile collection units (known as Bloodmobiles), blood donation centers in major towns and cities, and workplace sessions set up by companies and organizations. To be eligible to donate blood, individuals must generally be in good health, weigh at least 50 kg (7 st 12 lb), and be aged between 17 and 60 years. Regular donors in good health may continue donating until the age of 70. Donors are encouraged to donate up to four times a year. Before donating, donors undergo a check of their iron levels to ensure they are not anemic. They are also required to complete a questionnaire to confirm it is safe for them to donate blood and that their blood is safe for transfusion to others. Once these checks are completed, the donor lies on a bed, and a sterile needle connected to a collection bag is inserted into their arm. The process is not painful, contrary to common perceptions. It typically takes 5–10 minutes to collect one unit of blood, which is approximately 470–480 milliliters, or just under a pint. After donating, donors are offered tea and biscuits to help replenish lost fluids and to allow staff to monitor them for any signs of lightheadedness or fainting, which can occur if the donor has not eaten or drunk enough beforehand. The entire donation session usually lasts between 45 minutes and one hour. In addition to whole blood donations, the NBS also collects platelets using machines called cell separators, typically located in city-center blood donation centers. These machines separate platelets from the blood and return the remaining components to the donor. Platelets are small cell fragments that play a crucial role in blood clotting and are essential in the treatment of cancer and leukemia. Since platelets have a short shelf life of only five days, maintaining a constant supply is critical. Donors can give platelets every two weeks, and each donation typically provides 2–3 adult doses. Collecting one adult dose of platelets through this method would otherwise require four whole blood donations. The NBS has faced criticism for its longstanding policy of banning men who have had sex with men (MSM) from donating blood. This policy has sparked protests from university students in England and Scotland, with some institutions, such as Birmingham University's Guild of Students, even banning the NBS from setting up recruitment stalls during events like Freshers' Week. NBS officials defend the policy, citing safety concerns. Despite rigorous screening for infections, no test is 100% accurate, and MSM are considered at higher risk of carrying blood-transmitted diseases such as HIV. According to 2005 statistics from the Health Protection Agency, one-third of newly diagnosed HIV cases in the UK were among MSM, the highest numbers recorded since the start of the epidemic. MSM also account for 46% of all HIV diagnoses since 1981. The NBS also restricts donations from heterosexual individuals who have engaged in high-risk sexual practices, as well as those who have recently undergone acupuncture, tattoos, or piercings, or have traveled to countries with high rates of HIV infection.
